summaries.headline: Colorado Religious Public School Drops Discrimination Lawsuit
summaries.summary: Riverstone Academy and its authorizer dropped their federal religious discrimination lawsuit against Colorado less than four months after filing, with the case terminated Monday. The school's lawyer cited changes to state law limiting public education co-ops as making the case moot, potentially forcing Riverstone to close despite receiving state funding this year. The lawsuit's end derails what backers hoped would become a Supreme Court case establishing religious schools within public education systems, though similar efforts continue in other states.

summaries.headline: NYC Computer Science Push Falls Short on Equity Goals
summaries.summary: New York City's decade-old Computer Science for All initiative has expanded access dramatically, with more than 90% of schools now offering computer science classes compared to a handful in 2014, but enrollment remains at just 20% of students citywide. Only 1 in 5 schools are meeting the program's equity goals for girls, Latino, and Black students, despite overall enrollment quadrupling from 54,000 to more than 193,000 students. Education policy experts argue the city needs to pivot toward computational thinking and AI literacy rather than traditional coding as artificial intelligence reshapes the tech job market.

summaries.headline: Norwood Elementary Redesigns Reading Instruction Around Science-Based Practices
summaries.summary: Norwood Elementary in Stanly County transformed its literacy approach by implementing structured literacy practices rooted in the science of reading, moving away from balanced literacy methods that weren't serving all students effectively. The school restructured its instructional day to include explicit phonics instruction, systematic vocabulary development, and data-driven interventions while training teachers in evidence-based reading methods. The shift represents how elementary schools can operationalize research-backed literacy practices within existing constraints, providing a roadmap for districts grappling with similar reading proficiency challenges.

summaries.headline: Fifth Graders Learn Financial Literacy Through Celebrity AI
summaries.summary: Fifth graders at KIPP BOLD Academy in Newark are using ChatGPT to learn money management skills, asking AI to respond as their favorite celebrities while exploring concepts like needs versus wants and intentional saving. The classroom approach comes as New Jersey requires financial literacy for grades 6-8 and state senators push legislation to mandate a high school financial literacy course for graduation. The playful integration of technology with practical money skills reflects how schools are making financial education more engaging while addressing a growing national priority — 30 states now require financial education for graduation.

summaries.headline: AI Expands From Digital Monitoring to Physical School Surveillance
summaries.summary: School districts are deploying artificial intelligence beyond traditional content filtering and online activity monitoring to track student movements through digital hall passes, analyze cafeteria traffic patterns, and monitor campus entry points. The technology promises enhanced safety through early intervention capabilities—identifying behavioral incident patterns at specific locations and times to guide staff deployment decisions. This shift from digital to physical monitoring creates new privacy challenges that existing education privacy laws, designed for academic records and learning data, weren't built to address.

summaries.headline: Financial Pressures Force Budget Cuts Across Major Districts
summaries.summary: More than half of America's 50 largest school districts are making cuts or facing deficits as they prepare budgets for the upcoming school year, according to a Chalkbeat analysis. Districts cite a convergence of pressures including declining enrollment (nearly 30 of the largest 50 districts affected), rising healthcare costs driven partly by expensive weight-loss medications, and inflation in transportation and other operational expenses. The budget strain is translating into teacher layoffs, school closures, and increased class sizes as districts with enrollment-based funding struggle to maintain services with fewer students.

summaries.headline: Oklahoma's New Superintendent Aims to Rebuild After Walters Era
summaries.summary: State Superintendent Lindel Fields is working to restore stability to Oklahoma's public education system after his predecessor Ryan Walters left the role in September following 33 months of controversial MAGA-style policies that included mandatory Bible instruction, book bans, and ideological testing for teachers. Walters' tenure drew dozens of lawsuits and national attention while creating what educators describe as a climate of fear and targeting within school districts. Fields, who is finishing Walters' term but not seeking election, represents a deliberate shift toward what he calls "building a foundation" for public education — signaling how deeply political warfare has disrupted basic educational operations in one of the nation's most contested state systems.

summaries.headline: AI Push Risks Undermining Knowledge-Based Critical Thinking
summaries.summary: Education leaders are emphasizing critical thinking skills to prepare students for an AI-dominated world, but many professional development sessions treat these skills as separate from content knowledge. The American Federation of Teachers' new AI training initiative, backed by major tech companies, focuses on abstract thinking strategies while largely overlooking research showing that critical thinking depends on extensive domain-specific knowledge in subjects like math, history, and science. Schools risk weakening the very foundation—factual fluency—that cognitive scientists say enables students to think critically about complex, open-ended problems.

summaries.headline: OpenAI Expands Government Education Partnerships Across Three Countries
summaries.summary: OpenAI outlined its Education for Countries initiative at the London Education World Forum, detailing government partnerships that provide secure AI tools, teacher training, and research-backed deployments across national education systems. The program now operates in Estonia with more than 20,000 students and 4,600 teachers using ChatGPT Edu, selected 21 AI startups in Greece from 240 applications, and supports over 1 million students in Jordan through its Siraj platform. George Osborne, OpenAI's Head of Countries, emphasized that student-led adoption is already happening, positioning policy work around evidence and implementation rather than whether AI belongs in schools.

summaries.headline: Districts Must Separate Phone Bans From Instructional Technology
summaries.summary: District leaders face mounting pressure to ban devices as parents worry about screen time and academic performance, but the debate conflates personal smartphones with school-issued instructional technology. Nearly 9 in 10 schools operate one-to-one programs where students use computers or tablets for lessons, exams, and homework within carefully managed ecosystems that include content filtering and educational software. The distinction between behavior management issues with personal phones and legitimate learning opportunities with district devices will determine whether years of intentional technology investment survive the current policy conversation.

summaries.headline: Cloud Security Requires Human Training, Not Just Tech
summaries.summary: School districts face a 92% jump in ransomware attacks between 2022 and 2023 as cloud-based systems create new vulnerabilities rooted in human behavior rather than technology gaps. Cybersecurity expert Helen Patton notes that schools often misunderstand their responsibility for data security in cloud environments, assuming providers handle all protection while staff lack awareness of their role in maintaining security protocols. Districts are shifting toward treating cybersecurity awareness training, phishing simulations, and digital citizenship programs as routine operational safeguards rather than occasional IT initiatives.

summaries.headline: Private Schools Seek Court Protection in Funding Lawsuit
summaries.summary: Parents and private schools are asking to intervene in a lawsuit challenging Wisconsin's school finance system, arguing the case threatens the state's $700 million voucher program. The plaintiffs claim Wisconsin's funding system violates the constitution partly because money flows to private schools while public schools remain underfunded, citing a 2000 state Supreme Court ruling that choice programs are only permitted when the state meets its public school obligations. The intervention request signals how constitutional challenges to state funding formulas increasingly put voucher programs in the crosshairs, forcing courts to weigh competing claims about resource allocation across public and private education.

summaries.headline: Wisconsin Voters Still Prioritize School Funding, Property Tax Relief
summaries.summary: Wisconsin voters continue to rank property tax relief and school funding among their top policy priorities, according to the latest Marquette Law School poll. The polling data suggests these education finance issues remain politically salient for state lawmakers as they navigate budget decisions and potential reforms to the state's funding formula. The persistent voter concern signals that education funding debates will likely influence upcoming legislative sessions and electoral campaigns across the state.

summaries.headline: Newark Students Gain Fast but Remain Two Grades Behind
summaries.summary: Newark Public Schools students learned at a rate of 1.23 grade levels per year from 2022 to 2025, placing the district in the 93rd percentile nationally for academic growth according to a new Harvard-Stanford-Dartmouth study. The learning rate outpaced both national averages and similar urban districts like Camden and Trenton, which averaged eight-tenths of a grade level annually. Newark students still perform 2.36 grade levels below the 2019 national average, underscoring how even accelerated recovery leaves districts managing both momentum and substantial academic gaps.

summaries.headline: Mississippi College Partners to Train Delta Literacy Teachers
summaries.summary: Coahoma Community College launched a regional partnership with Reading Roadmap, Inc. to deliver evidence-based literacy training for K-3 educators across five Mississippi Delta counties. The initiative uses a train-the-trainer model covering emotional intelligence, data-driven decision making, and family engagement, with participating districts receiving full curriculum sets at no cost. The collaboration positions the historically Black community college as a hub for instructional leadership in a region where early literacy gains could reshape educational trajectories for thousands of students.

summaries.headline: North Carolina Targets Chronic Absenteeism With New Pilot
summaries.summary: North Carolina lawmakers are developing a pilot program to address chronic student absenteeism as 400,000 students across the state missed a month or more of school. The legislative initiative comes as chronic absenteeism rates continue to challenge districts statewide, affecting roughly one in four students based on the scale described. The targeted approach signals growing recognition that attendance interventions require systematic, policy-level support rather than leaving individual schools to tackle the crisis alone.

summaries.headline: Trump Budget Would Fold Rural Ed Funding Into Block Grants
summaries.summary: The Trump administration wants to eliminate the $220 million Rural Education Achievement Program and roll it into a $2 billion block grant that would give governors and state education chiefs discretion over funding distribution. Rural superintendents say they depend on the dedicated federal dollars for essential services like technology coordinators and teaching assistants for struggling students, with one North Dakota district using its $14,000 allocation to fund academic support staff. District leaders worry that folding rural-specific funding into broader state allocations would mean larger districts absorb the money, leaving small rural schools without reliable resources for core operational needs.

summaries.headline: Cybersecurity Tops AI Concerns for Education Tech Leaders
summaries.summary: Education technology leaders nationwide identify AI-enabled cyber attacks as their primary concern about artificial intelligence in schools, according to the latest State of Ed Tech report from the Consortium for School Networking (CoSN). The survey findings highlight how data privacy and security vulnerabilities overshadow other AI implementation challenges as districts navigate the technology's rapid adoption. School leaders now face the dual challenge of harnessing AI's educational benefits while protecting increasingly sophisticated attack vectors that could compromise sensitive student and district data.
summaries.source_name: THE Journal: Technological Horizons in Education

summaries.headline: Oakland Awards $5,000 for Perfect Attendance
summaries.summary: Oakland Unified awarded a McClymonds High School senior $5,000 for nearly perfect attendance as part of efforts to combat chronic absenteeism that peaked at 53% during the pandemic. Districtwide chronic absenteeism has improved to 29%, though Black students still account for more than 41% of chronically absent students despite declining enrollment in the district. The cash incentive reflects how districts are testing direct financial rewards to address attendance patterns that researchers link to broader equity challenges beyond traditional interventions.

local_articles.title: RSU 12 Approves Education Budget in Half an Hour
local_articles.summary: RSU 12 Approves Education Budget in Half an Hour  The Lincoln County News
local_articles.full_content:
Voters approved RSU 12’s $30 million education budget for the upcoming fiscal year in just 30 minutes at a meeting on Wednesday, May 20.

The RSU 12 Board of Directors recommended the $30,038,306.13 budget for the upcoming fiscal year at a meeting on April 10. The amount is a $1,397,579.31 or 4.8% increase from last fiscal year.

Before voting, RSU 12 Superintendent Howard Tuttle gave a presentation of the budget and explained how the final total was decided, as well as how it will affect the seven participating towns in the school district.

All warrant articles passed with zero discussion.

Taxpayers in the district’s towns will be responsible for $16,810,192.96, an increase of $698,676.78 or 4.2%.

Whitefield’s share is $3,260,332.51, an increase of $165,687.73 or 5.8%. Alna will be responsible for $1,284,870.39, an increase of $69,385.88 or 5.2%. Somerville will be responsible for $774,786.05, an increase of $5,363 or 0.6%. Westport Island’s share is $1,118,094.76, an increase of $61,692.31 or 5.8%.

Chelsea’s contribution will be $3,315,890.64, an increase of $84,342.02 or 2.6%. Palermo’s responsibility totals $2,557,573.96, an increase of $104,051.06 or 4.2%. Windsor will contribute for $4,398,644.65, an increase of $298,156.34 or 4.9%.

During the meeting, Tuttle said some notable areas of change include the transportation and buses budget, as well as the facilities and maintenance budget.

“It hasn’t been the easiest time to create a budget,” Tuttle said.

The transportation and buses budget totals $1,862,385.22, an increase of $59,301.60 or 3.29%.Tuttle said the budget factors in anticipated rising fuel costs.

The $2,344,295.53 facilities and maintenance budget is an increase of $192,381.87 or 8.94%. Tuttle said the budgeted amount is for roof repairs at Whitefield Elementary School.

Over 70% of the budget is allocated for regular instruction, secondary tuition, and special education. The recommended regular instruction budget totals $6,508,229, an increase of $128,883.51 or 2%. Tuition for secondary education is budgeted at $8,734,625.75, an increase of $612,523.55 or 7.5%. Special education is budgeted at $6,311,880.43, an increase of $190,458.75 or 3.11%.

Other areas of the budget include other instruction at $179,660, an increase of $22,001.95 or 13.96%; student and staff support at $1,353,698.69, an increase of $45,115.53 or 3.44%; system administration at $825,968.77, an increase of $64,024.89 or 8.40%; school administration at $1,063,460.39, an increase of $72,887.66 or 7.36%; transportation and buses at $1,862,385.22, an increase of $59,301.60 or 3.29%; and debt service at $854,102.35, an increase of $10,000 or 1.18%.

Tuttle also mentioned the possibility of Liberty leaving RSU 3 and joining RSU 12. Students from Liberty would attend Palermo Consolidated School without the need of adding more teachers and staff. If Liberty were to join RSU 12, Tuttle said each town in the school district’s contribution would drop by at least 5%.

The conversation for the transition is ongoing, and there have not been any decisions made yet, he said.

Voters will consider validating the budget at their polling locations on Tuesday, June 9.

For more information, call 549-3261 or go to [svrsu.org](http://svrsu.org/).

local_articles.title: Benedict: Act 955 kicks school funding can down the road, again
local_articles.summary: Benedict: Act 955 kicks school funding can down the road, again  Vermont Daily Chronicle
local_articles.full_content:
![](<Base64-Image-Removed>)![](https://i0.wp.com/vermontdailychronicle.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/62uud64b.png?fit=639%2C479&ssl=1)

**By Chaunce Benedict**

Well, there you go! Act 955, the public-school transformation bill, as amended promises “substantial equity…delivered at a cost that parents, voters and taxpayers will value.” Just what will the “transformation” be?

Turning down the verbal volume, there will be…

– Many committees “studying” mergers. Many tens of thousands of hours of meetings. Many paid consultants. No mergers are assured. Will need two + years to study. And, for just the cost of a few hundred thousand dollars.

– A new administrative superstructure of “Cooperative Educational Service Areas”. To do things that are already being done. More efficiently and effectively. For sure. No doubt.

– A “new foundation formula”. Just like the “maps” required by Act 73. Remember those?

– An effort to enact legislation that expresses clear “intent” related to “career and technical education, special education funding, sparsity, empirically supported secondary student weighting, geographic cost differences, a pre-K funding mechanism, legacy collective bargaining agreements, and capital indebtedness held by school districts.” All ought to be taken care of expediently and with minimal difficulty, right? No question.

– And, reports. Lots of reports. Merger committee facilitator reports. A foundation formula report. A State Board of Education Report. All reports will most certainly be read carefully and taken to heart. These will make a real difference, correct?

– School construction. The funds for it: piece of cake. Money grows on trees.

Anything in here, beyond a few throw away rhetorical phrases, about improving learning, reading, etc.? Please show us.

According to the powers-that-be, all of this will be just exactly what Vermonters say they want. Really? Just who?

Remember Act 46? Really improved learning and schools, at a cost “Vermonters will support”. Right?

So now comes Act 955. Another kick of the can down the road? Sadly for Vermont, probably yes.

# Education budget review exposes gaps in teacher welfare cover

Thursday 28th May, 2026 08:21 AM\|By [Kenneth Mwenda](https://peopledaily.digital/author/kennethmwenda "Posts by Kenneth Mwenda")

![Education budget review exposes gaps in teacher welfare cover](https://peopledaily.digital/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/G0tvTEXXQAA0TLT-768x528.jpeg)Teachers at State House on Saturday, September 13, 2025. PHOTO/@WilliamsRuto/X

The Budget and Appropriations Committee has raised concern over gaps in teacher welfare coverage, especially the absence of key insurance protections, during its review of education sector allocations for the 2026/27 financial year.

The committee, chaired by Samuel Atandi, is examining proposed estimates totalling Ksh4.82 trillion. It heard submissions from the Departmental Committee on Education, the Parliamentary Service Commission and the Committee on Blue Economy, Water and Irrigation.

The Teachers Service Commission (TSC) has been allocated a proposed Ksh422 billion. The funds will support the promotion of about 30,000 teachers, conversion of 20,000 intern teachers to permanent and pensionable terms, retraining of 120,000 teachers under the Competency-Based Education (CBE) programme, and implementation of the second phase of the 2025–2029 Collective Bargaining Agreement.

## Unresolved welfare issues

However, MPs focused on unresolved welfare issues affecting teachers, with particular concern over delayed pension payments and missing insurance cover.

[![Treasury defends Ksh4.78T budget amid MPs’ revenue and spending scrutiny](https://peopledaily.digital/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/mba44-225x141.png)](https://peopledaily.digital/business/treasury-defends-ksh4-78t-budget-amid-mps-revenue-and-spending-scrutiny)

The committee noted that the budget has no provision for group life insurance, group personal accident cover, and Work Injury Benefits Act (WIBA) insurance for teachers. Lawmakers said these protections would cost about Ksh5.3 billion but remain unfunded.

Members warned that leaving out these covers exposes teachers to financial risk, especially in cases of injury, disability or death while on duty.

Lawmakers also pointed out that after the shift of teachers’ medical cover from private insurers to the Social Health Authority (SHA), the government saved nearly Ksh4 billion annually. They proposed that part of these savings should go towards funding insurance protection for teachers.

On basic education, the committee noted persistent funding gaps despite the sector receiving the largest share of the national budget. Capitation remains a key pressure point.

“Basic education is a sector that has the largest resource allocation. We have capitation figures in secondary education of about Ksh54 billion, junior secondary around Ksh30 billion and primary education around Ksh7 billion,” said Education Committee Chair Hon. Julius Melly.

![Teachers during the ceremony at Kenya Methodist University, Meru County. PHOTO/https://www.facebook.com/Kithure KindikI](https://peopledaily.digital/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/704851286_1536296334780871_7396034104159500510_n-Cropped-500x500.jpg)Teachers during the ceremony at Kenya Methodist University, Meru County. PHOTO/https://www.facebook.com/Kithure KindikI

## MPs push education reforms

The State Department for Basic Education has been allocated Ksh135.3 billion for schools, examinations, school feeding programmes, infrastructure and quality assurance.

MPs also questioned the current school placement system, saying some schools remain overcrowded while others operate below capacity.

The committee backed proposals to improve the school feeding programme, including fresh mapping of beneficiary areas and better inclusion of learners with special needs. It also recommended that the National Council for Nomadic Education in Kenya (NACONEK) remap targeted regions and set clear inclusion guidelines.

Lawmakers further supported direct disbursement of co-curricular funds to schools to avoid delays that disrupt sports, music and drama activities under CBE.

The State Department for Higher Education will receive Ksh164.1 billion, while MPs noted ongoing concerns around scholarship funding under the new model.

![Part of the statement from Parliament on teachers’ welfare. PHOTO/Screengrab by People Daily Digital](https://peopledaily.digital/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Screenshot-2026-05-28-074922.png)Part of the statement from Parliament on teachers’ welfare. PHOTO/Screengrab by People Daily Digital

In technical education, the committee welcomed an increase in TVET capitation from Ksh3.5 billion to over Ksh9 billion.

“This time it has been raised to over Ksh9 billion for TVET students, and this is actually to ensure that they go back to colleges and we are able to fund them,” said John Chikati.

The government has announced a major boost in teacher promotions, with Deputy President Kithure Kindiki confirming [that](https://peopledaily.digital/news/kindiki-announces-promotion-of-50k-teachers-in-new-budget) [50,000 teachers will be promoted in the coming financial year](https://peopledaily.digital/news/kindiki-announces-promotion-of-50k-teachers-in-new-budget). He said the decision follows increased budgetary allocation and consultations with education stakeholders, including teachers’ unions.

“In this budget, I confirm that we have factored in money for promotions. Initially, the target was 25,000 teachers. You informed the President that the number was not enough, and the government will now be promoting 50,000 teachers,” Kindiki said.

The committee also called for an audit of equipment in TVET institutions to redistribute idle machinery and strengthen training capacity.

Members maintained that stronger education financing remains key to improving teacher welfare, expanding access, and supporting the rollout of CBE across the country.
